item.description:
Ubisoft is clearly serious about implementing generative-AI deeply into the game development process. The French publisher now expects teams pitching new project ideas to be prepared to explain how gen-AI will help with developing the game.Teams who don't want to use gen-AI will need to clearly justify their reasoning to the higher-ups.
That's according to a new Vertical Slice report, citing multiple anonymous sources currently working at Ubisoft.
Several employees said that pitching a game idea without gen-AI or without explaining why it does not involve the use of the controversial tech will not receive the greenlight. This is especially relevant for smaller games with tight teams who now reportedly must deal with Ubisoft leaders' desire to implement gen-AI if they want to get their pitches reviewed.
"We were told that using AI will increase the speed at which pitches can be made by 'small lean agile teams,'" one source said. "We were told that as the goal was to move fast, iterate and discard projects to sift out the good stuff. AI was essential in maintaining a rapid pace."
While some said Ubisoft is not openly mandating gen-AI use to staff, others feel "cornered" by gen-AI. One source said Ubisoft views the tech as "unavoidable", and that only a minority of the company's audience reject it.
Ubisoft recently gave name to an internal initiative to expand the use of generative-AI and research how its developers can make use of the technology. It's called Motherbrain, and it has its own division within Ubisoft.
Over a year ago, Ubisoft embarked on a major restructuring effort that has seen the formation of new subsidiaries, the consolidation of its biggest brands into 'creative houses', the closure of studios and, of course, multiple rounds of layoffs.
"Ubisoft is in a top-down nightmare of AI psychosis," one source added, pointing to the already low morale within the company. "Yves [Guillemot] has hitched his wagon to the tech, demanding the rest of the company follow on."

item.title: Many World of Warcraft: Forever players are currently in the midst of a substantial PvP reputation grind. However, this process has been disrupted due to a sudden change to one of the game's battleground PvP arenas. Read more
item.description:
Many World of Warcraft: Forever players are currently in the midst of a substantial PvP reputation grind. However, this process has been disrupted due to a sudden change to one of the game's battleground PvP arenas.
The battleground in question is Alterac Valley, a 40 person-a-side clash between Alliance and Horde factions, where both sides need to push their forces across a snowy, mountainous map into the opposing faction's base to take down the NPC General waiting there. Alterac Valley is being grinded by max-level players for its gear rewards that are given once reaching "exalted" reputation there. Currently it's some of the best gear available ahead of raids being introduced next month.
Played the intended way, Alterac Valley is a lengthy battle. The Generals on both sides are fearsomely tough but by rushing to capture certain structures on the way to this battle, you can weaken the Generals enough to make them easier to overcome. As such, players have been fast-tracking this PvP instance, skipping smaller objectives and rushing core objectives to get to the Generals as fast as possible. This bypassed a lot of the incidental skirmishing allure of Alterac Valley, but it was an efficient way to quickly gain reputation and Honor points (PvP currency).
But this strategy has been pretty much killed outright as of today. In a post made to the official World of Warcraft forums, community manager Kaivax revealed that the reputation gained from killing the Generals has been drastically reduced, while the reputation gained from killing other NPCs and capturing previously ignored objectives now grants more. Generals are also granted a buff that makes them incredibly strong for the first 20 minutes of a match, which is then reduced for each objective taken.
This is a good change in regard to the experience of playing Alterac Valley. While rushing through was good for players looking to gain reputation quickly, they weren't really playing the Battleground in the way it's meant to be played. The dev post reads: "The overall intent for all of these changes was for games to feel more meaningful while trying to maintain a similar amount of rep gained over a similar playtime within the battleground, even with longer match lengths. There will be fluctuations depending on how successful you are at destroying towers and holding capture points at the end of a match however."
It appears as of writing that the reputation gained isn't as much as it was previously, so those playing purely for reputation have been hit. There's another element of frustration which is that those who rushed to level 60 and ground Alterac Valley reputation and rewards before the changes won't be affected by this. Perhaps that's the allure of rushing to level 60!
"This is why the WoW mantra is 'exploit early, exploit often'," writes user Lanienah12. "Some people are already exalted with AV rep and will receive no punishment for it; meanwhile new people will be spending 3x as long." Especially in the wake of the Blackmaw Hold gold exploit being discovered by these frontrunners, there's a growing belief that those taking their time or that are limited by real-life factors are feeling the brunt of these changes.

item.title: Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up  to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6. Read more
item.description:
Despite the far higher prices of PlayStation and Xbox consoles today compared to their launch, or even the same period last year, both brands of console saw a significant boost in US sales leading up to the launch of this generation's biggest game: Grand Theft Auto 6.
In the week ending 14th November, PS5 hardware unit sales registered a 2.4x increase over the same week last year. Xbox wasn't far behind, seeing a 2.3x increase in its own unit sales. That's according to industry analyst Mat Piscatella at Circana, who pulled the data from Circana's retail tracking service, which covers the US retail market.
The PS5 Pro only accounted for less than 10 percent of the PlayStation's total unit sales, by the way, which Piscatella noted was "a LOT better than it has been in recent weeks", and seemingly the result of increased supply.
GTA 6, of course, released on 19th November, so the surge in console hardware sales was clearly driven by the rush to attain consoles before the game came out. And while the GTA 6-driven demand isn't surprising, it's worth noting how much more expensive PS5 and Xbox Series X/S consoles are today.
A standard PS5 today costs $650, compared to $550 a year ago. The PS5 Pro saw a big jump from $750 last November to $900 today. The base Xbox Series X jumped from $650 last year to $800 today, while Series S now costs $500, up from $400.
Even Switch 2, where GTA 6 is not available, saw a notable boost of 40 percent in hardware sales over the same period, driven by The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake and the special edition Zelda Switch 2 console.
Circana's November US video game market report, which releases in December, is already one of the most anticipated this year, for digesting and documenting the GTA 6 effect. Worldwide, GTA 6 sold more than 32.5m copies in one day, making Rockstar's parent company Take-Two $3.79bn (£2.89bn) in revenue. We haven't had any updated official sales figures since; but estimates suggest the sales figure could be well into the 40-millions. Perhaps Rockstar is waiting to hit the nice round 50m sales mark before announcing it.
If you're playing GTA 6, you may want to keep Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough to hand. It has plenty of very helpful guides covering the game's main missions, as well as explainers for mechanics like romance and the criminal profile, and even cheats for when you finish the game.

item.title: Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their big RPGs and set a new "gold standard." Read more
item.description:
Developer Playground Games had to look beyond Lionhead's original run of Fable games when rebooting the classic fantasy series, and it's all thanks to games like The Witcher 3, which changed what many players expect from their big RPGs and set a new "gold standard."
The upcoming Fable reboot is finally ending its decade-long development journey soon. Playground Games had to set up an entirely new team to work on its fairytale revival, so Fable's production wasn't quite as smooth sailing as the studio's consistently excellent Forza Horizon series, for example.
Asked about what's changed during that time, in an interview with GamesIndustry.biz, studio founder and general manager Ralph Fulton named technological advancements as a biggie, but the impact of other games was perhaps even greater.
"In 2015, The Witcher 3 redefined what an open-world action RPG looks like and became the gold standard," Fulton said. "And after that bar was raised, the Assassin's Creed franchise changed into this more modern iteration with Origins, Odyssey, and Valhalla, and became like a quasi-RPG."
"All of these games continue to reset player expectations," he continued. Millions of players suddenly had certain expectations about what their big-budget, open-world role-playing games should look like. So, Playground couldn't pull inspiration from Fable and Fable alone.
"I think looking only to the original Fable trilogy for inspiration would leave us lacking in terms of what the modern audience, the modern marketplace, expects," Fulton added.
Still, Playground's Fable is drawing most heavily from Lionhead's Fable. Fulton specifically mentions the game's signature British wit and in-flux morality system as examples. Then there's also the spontaneous life sim elements that "none of our competitors do," according to Fulton. "It's a totally Fable thing, the social simulation and economic simulation. Okay, there are games that have economic simulations, but they're not in [our] RPG category. Fable is unique in that it's almost like a life sim in terms of genre."
Raising four separate families and becoming the entire map's benevolent landlord was one of the funnest parts of Fable back in the day, alongside those sometimes silly characters. Seeing next year's Fable lean into those systemic choices, and having Albion's NPCs react to them more believably, could give this one a very long shelf life.

item.title: Action game maestro Hideki Kamiya really wants to make a new Castlevania game with publisher Konami. Read more
item.description:
Action game maestro Hideki Kamiya really wants to make a new Castlevania game with publisher Konami.
The long-time developer best known for his work in the director's chair on a host of beloved games - Bayonetta, Resident Evil 2, Okami, Devil May Cry and The Wonderful 101 included - recently published a new video to his personal YouTube account. While the video was first recorded last year, it does give us some hints on what Kamiya is interested in making after his in-development Okami sequel wraps up.
Perhaps the most noteworthy tidbit came from Kamiya advocating to make a new game in Konami's vampiric action-adventure series. "We'll definitely make Castlevania. If you let us work on it, we can make something truly insane, so just contact us and we'll be at your service," Kamiya said. (Thanks, Automaton!)
Kamiya presumably has his hands full with Capcom's Okami 2, which is currently in production at the director's newfound independent studio Clovers. Needless to say, any potential Kamiya-led Castlevania game will likely need to wait in a coffin for a while more.
In the meantime, it's not like Castlevania has remained dormant and defanged. Earlier this year, Konami promised that "numerous new products around Castlevania" are in the pipeline. While new games weren't explicitly confirmed, it's safe to assume Konami would be interested in hearing pitches from outside devs. Kamiya can stay hopeful knowing that Evil Empire just dropped another gorgeous, aggressive action-platformer in the series.
"Like Rose herself, the game is earnest, intelligent, and capable of brilliance. But, mimicking its protagonist, it is also awkward, and unable to fully come to terms with its own unique identity in the shadow of its over-bearing legacy," Dom wrote in Eurogamer's Castlevania: Belmont's Curse review. "By no means is Belmont's Curse a bad game, I just think Evil Empire sunk its teeth a bit too deep into something it wasn't quite ready to consume."
This isn't the first time Kamiya has publicly expressed interest in reviving older games, either. He recently said he's "100% serious" about bringing back Scalebound, his cancelled Xbox One exclusive.

item.title: EA Sports FC 27 is using gen-AI to digitally recreate the voice of veteran football commentator John Motson - the FIFA video game series' first ever real-world announcer who died in 2023. Read more
item.description:
But EA's now decided to digitally resurrect Motson - or, at least, his incredibly recognisable voice - with permission from his family. An update with Motson's voice will go live on 26th November. "There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," senior game designer director Mat Prior said in a statement given to the BBC earlier today.
Fred Motson said it "means an awful lot" to hear his dad's voice in the game again, and he reckons his dad was "always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects," even if he wasn't the most technologically savvy person. EA said it had paid the family for the rights to use Motson's voice and likeness.
Save Our Voices Now founder Peter Caulfield - who campaigns for the government to regulate the use of generative AI voice cloning tech - told the BBC he wasn't comfortable with the project. "In life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed," he said. "Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either." He doesn't have a problem with actors consenting to AI voice replication while they're still alive, however.
A Japanese acting union recently fought back against this very same practice by proposing new guidelines that would stop the replication of dead actors' voices without their permission.
Generative AI has been widely controversial in the games industry for other reasons, too. In recent months, there's been a huge impact on smaller game developers who are worried that their games could be cloned by AI copycats and some who have had to delay their release dates because of Steam's growing approvals backlog.
"The Grounds comes across as a frippery, Ultimate Team rumbles ever on, but FC 27 brings meaningful changes to the fluidity and speed of play. Given that its practical football-game monopoly is more or less unchallenged, EA could do a lot less than this," Josh Wise wrote in Eurogamer's EA Sports FC 27 review.

item.title: There's been plenty of chatter about Grand Theft Auto 6's 'honour system', so to speak, implemented here via what the game calls your Criminal Profile. Read more
item.description:
There's been plenty of chatter about Grand Theft Auto 6's 'honour system', so to speak, implemented here via what the game calls your Criminal Profile.
Our own Dom just wrote that they prefer to turn its notifications off, for instance, in favour of fully soaking into the immersion. Personally I quite like the pop-ups - I find the act of figuring out systems and how they're manipulated almost as fun as the games they're a part of. And pop-ups or no, the fact that GTA 6 can arguably be portrayed as 'rewarding' empathy and 'discouraging' the series' famous rampages of mass violence has sparked a fair bit of debate.
Some of that is genuinely interesting - I'm dubious as to whether that's really what this system is doing, for a start. Is it incentivising and disincentivising certain in-game behaviour, or just putting a label on it? And then, actually: does the act of labelling "psycho" behaviour alone actually become a disincentivising factor in itself?
Either way, until now Rockstar hasn't said a great deal about why, exactly, this system - seen by some as one that builds empathy into GTA's chaotic world - was implemented in the first place. But during an interview I had with Rob Nelson, Rockstar Games' head of development, just before GTA 6's launch earlier this month, a little more on that came to light.
A little context is necessary here: Nelson's response was actually following a question I had about the overall approach to design that Rockstar took, and how its wider themes and intentions came about. As a part of that, he turned to this system - and how, in a way, it exists here because of the work the studio simply didn't want to leave behind after Red Dead Redemption 2.
Nelson explained that this all began when the team was in the early phase of exploring what type of game GTA 6 would be, in 2015 and 2016, while much of the studio was still working full-tilt on RDR2 - a game which itself didn't release until late 2018. The team was looking to "build up the sophistication of the NPC population, and also allow for more player choice than we had [before], and more options in terms of the way you interact with the world beyond just violence," Nelson told me.
The idea would be that "it's still a world of violence - but you could threaten somebody by aiming a gun at them and just robbing them, and they have a chance to comply. So you don't have to beat them to death to get their money." Ideas that were "simple things" in principle, he said, "but they create a lot more work in terms of development of the sophistication of the systems."
Then, as systems were gradually implemented, it became a question of "trying to marry up what you're doing in the open world with who we're saying you are in the narrative - more than we had, I would say, previously, in Red Dead 2." It's here where the system now referred to as the Criminal Profile started to form.
The thinking turned to "the nature of 'honour', which wasn't always a part of it" with Red Dead Redemption 2, Nelson continued, "but became part of it as we were working on this story and finding that the 'redemption arc' didn't feel so good when it was foisted upon you - and feelings that we had playing Red Dead sort of early on." (Those feelings, primarily, were around getting you to invest in a gang led by Dutch Van der Linde, who was fundamentally unlikable from the off - or plain "crazy", as Nelson put it. The implementation of more player choices and agency was part of Rockstar's way to build investment in Arthur, even as he followed Dutch.)
That meant moving the choices away from key story moments, where many games tend to put them. Instead, Rockstar built a system that ran alongside the story via smaller, moment-to-moment choices you might make. "We tried to take all of those off the main flow and make them optional. So again, they're a choice."
"Usually they involve some form of slight sacrifice or more effort on the part of the player," he added. The hope, then, was that you as a player would both "feel something", and ultimately also feel "you got the outcome that you deserved."
That was the initial thinking behind this kind of system as a whole. Coming to GTA 6, it then combined with a wider desire to "evolve" Grand Theft Auto as both the team's storytelling and the available technology matured. "You're thinking about story and character set, but we're also thinking about what we want to do with GTA as a series, and how you want to evolve it," Nelson said.
"I think as the resolution goes up, it sort of asks different new questions," he continued. "As the resolution goes up, you want the sophistication of the experience to go up, and obviously the sophistication of the mechanics. So it just naturally flowed that we give players choices to interact with the world beyond just violence, beyond just 'down the barrel of a gun', because it's fun."
"It's fun for some people like myself to just sort of role-play in the world, and be in the world, and restraint becomes something you hadn't thought about," he continued. That tied back into the more sophisticated NPCs and reactions the team were making.
"If you think about the NPCs, even back to [GTA] 5, you would draw a weapon - first of all, they didn't react if you drew an invisible shotgun out of nowhere, or a rocket launcher," he said. "They don't react unless you aim it, and then they flee in terror, and you're just sort of this demigod stomping through the world, you know? And that's fun, but for how long?
"The team then started thinking of ways to build a bit more sustained enjoyment from it. "What if you can't do that?" Nelson continued. What if, instead of whipping an RPG out of nowhere, "you have to call your car. You have to pop a car trunk and get it, and now I'm walking, and now people are noticing, but they're sort of sidling away, and it's more believable. And then they're still fleeing in terror, but then there's people who also have guns, and they're shooting at you, or you try to hold somebody up and they pull a gun, or they grab it, and then you have to deal with them.
"And then, he continued, "you choose. You're trying to jack somebody off a motorcycle, and they pull a gun on you, and you have to blow their head off and it's like, 'You shouldn't have made me do that!' And so then it has more meaning, and it's more funny in a way when it's a little bit more pointed. And you can still go on those rampages and basically smash your Criminal Profile until it breaks and then you enter this irredeemable state, which basically says 'I reject your criminal profile system! I don't want it.'"
That Irredeemable profile level, for what it's worth, was another element born of Red Dead Redemption 2. "We had that with Red Dead, where people would sort of have low honour, and then 'greet' their way back up to high honour. And so this was an attempt of sorts of [making something] for people that just want to go crazy and almost opt out of the system. They can opt out of it - and you can also turn off the notifications in the system."
It's notable, in fact, just how interlinked the thinking was with GTA 6 and Red Dead Redemption 2. As Nelson put it at one point: "There was maybe more emotional resonance in the story of RDR2 than we had had, certainly in a GTA before. So we liked that idea." What Rockstar did with GTA 6 was then in a way a natural next step. "We didn't necessarily come to GTA 6 going: 'We must have emotional resonance,' but all of those things combine. It's more that those systems and that element of player choice and agency, and the way that affected the narrative, was a hard thing to ignore and walk away from."
We'll have much more like this from our interview with Nelson very soon, so do look out for that on Eurogamer over the coming days. In the meantime, we've a handy guide explaining exactly how GTA 6's Criminal Profile system works and how to change, raise, or lower that profile if you're in need of a deep dive into how it all really works.

As World of Warcraft: Forever players dived into the game, they quickly discovered a specific weapon enchant that took area of effect spells to a whole other level. Sadly, with a sudden hotfix last night, this particular use case for the enchant has been removed.
The enchantment in question was Revelation - a new addition to the game included as part of the new trade good reputations. What it does is simple: when you fail to deal a critical strike with a spell, the next spell hit is guaranteed to do so. What made this particularly powerful is that the buff also worked with continuous area of effect spells, meaning an early instance of the spell not crit-ing would result in the remaining damage hits all dealing critical damage.
So for example, let's say you're a druid casting the Hurricane spell. This is a channel spell with a total of 10 seconds of cast time. Every second, it deals damage. If the first instance of damage at the one second mark doesn't crit, the remaining nine instances of damage would all crit. This resulted in absurd amounts of damage, and made players of druids, warlocks, and mages very happy.
While strong enchantments are often pricey, this was notably cheap, due to the low-cost of resources used to create it and the low requirements to learn it. As such, people were spending a handful of gold for an early game enchantment that was being actively used all the way into the end game.
It was admittedly a tad too strong, and the effect triggered on AOE spells was almost certainly an unintended effect of the enchantment. Last night, the fun came to an end. Now, the effect is used up as intended in long-casted spells. So going back to the example given, if the first instance of damage on Hurricane doesn't crit, then the second one still will. However, this will use up the effect, and the third instance of damage will revert to regular ol' damage numbers. It also seems as though it Revelation can't trigger more than once during a single channeled spell.
This is the latest in a string of ongoing quickfire bug fixes and game adjustments being made to World of Warcraft: Forever. The devs have been continuously updating the game in an attempt to curb certain gold farms, following the discovery of a particularly lucrative Blackmaw Hold gold exploit. The dev team has expressed some interesting ideas for the game longterm, including a desire to kill best-in-slot gear.

item.description:
Hollow Knight: Silksong developer Team Cherry has announced it will host a 'Cherry Time Special Presentation' on 27th November, bringing more information to light about the game's first big DLC offering, Sea of Sorrows. We know that the free update will be nautically-themed - hence the eponymous 'sea' - and will feature new bosses, areas and so on, but other than that, information about what's coming is vague.
But it seems that's not all; as well as more information about the mysterious update to the hit Metroidvania game, the studio has also announced "a bunch" of other "exciting announcements." Curious.
The Cherry Time Special Presentation will kick off at 7am PT / 10am ET / 3pm GMT / 4pm CEST. I'll embed the video below, so check back here at the time if you need a bookmark.
Recently, and more than a year after its initial release, physical versions of Hollow Knight: Silksong finally began arriving on players' doorsteps. Whilst these editions contained mostly expected information, there was an unforeseen mention of "free content packs" that would be arriving alongside the Sea of Sorrow DLC. Will we hear more about these as part of this new showcase? We don't have too long to find out.
It seems likely, though. "The world of Hollow Knight: Silksong will expand with free content packs," the booklet read in the physical editions. "Prepare for even more adventures filled with new friends, new abilities, and new ferocious foes!" Team Cherry has repeatedly confirmed plans for post-launch Silksong support, but other than this upcoming DLC, we don't really know what that entails.
Additionally, Sea of Sorrow's original release window was a vague 2026 - will we see it shadowdrop as part of this stream? Stranger things have happened, especially in the world of Hollow Knight…

item.description:
Things continue to get messy in the community of players working on getting Grand Theft Auto 6 working on PC. The previous frontrunner, Project Leonida, got their Discord server and GitHub repository taken down by Rockstar, but others have seemingly stepped in to finish the job.
The most up-to-date build of GTA 6 was allegedly leaked earlier this week by notorious leaker CyberLeek. This is a supposedly near-final build of the game's Xbox version, and it's seemingly being used as the basis for the recent work to port the game to PC.
Unsurprisingly, most of these communities of modders rely almost exclusively on generative-AI tools like Claude and Antigravity to decompile and recompile the console version of GTA 6. That has always been the case, but the CyberLeek build only invited even more to ask AI chatbots to make the PC port for them.
X user chasm has been following developments in the GTA 6 decompile and recompile communities, and recently shared some of the prompts the so-called vibe-coders are using - a few of whom livestreamed the process.
"Make no mistakes," one modder prompted the AI chatbot. "Keep finding more stuff and working and pushing," another eloquently asked. "Work faster," asked another. "There has to be a faster way to iterate than this," they continued.
Rockstar, which successfully managed to DMCA take down Project Leonida - including all of its 3,006 forks on lead author NotRexed's GitHub - is seemingly also going after people online discussing the community's progress. The X user in question later revealed they may no longer be able to share these updates, as their posts have also been removed "in response to a report by the copyright owner".
As for how far some of the remaining communities have managed to get, this video allegedly shows the game running on PC. This goes beyond the boot-up screen, which modders were able to reach within hours of CyberLeek's build alleged leaking.
The footage runs at sub-5fps, but the visuals look to have rendered normally. Assuming Rockstar doesn't also shut down the modders who remain active, we may see another progress update.
If you're already playing Rockstar's latest on consoles, the Eurogamer GTA 6 walkthrough offers comprehensive guides on relationship mechanics, how the new Criminal Profile system works, a list of all safe codes and more.

item.title: Do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life? item.description:
Do you think you'd enjoy invasive UI elements in real life? You crouch to fuss your dog, and a little ping activates in your retina, informing you that you've just earned plus-three serotonin. Your boss chews you out for coming into work 15 minutes late thanks to a traffic accident holding you up on your way to work, a notification pings: "-10 percent motivation (lasts 24 hours)". Maybe you eat a bang-up meal, flirt with a hot stranger, beat your personal best on a run - ding, ding, ding. Well done, you win at being a human.
I think it'd be tortuous. I think it would interact with my already-questionable perception of reality, and send my neurodivergent coping mechanisms into overdrive. I already see time 'in blocks', and am incapable of breaking tasks down to anything less than 15 minute chunks - I can't imagine how ill I'd get if I could begin ascribing status buffs and debuffs to those blocks, too. We're all different, of course - such is the beauty of life - but I think most people would be pushed to the point of meltdown if every action they took had a quantifiable mechanical system attached to it.
So why is it any different in GTA 6? The game, after all, is the most effective simulation we've ever seen about modern life. Aside from the rampant crime sprees you can engage with, there's so much mundanity in the game it's beyond impressive: I spent the opening 10-or-so hours in the game with a very strict morning routine. I'd get up, work out, shower, feed Dolores the snake, drink a protein shake, then head to one of the local businesses to get some breakfast. Every day! I'm a busy person; I'm playing GTA 6 for fun, yes, but also as part of my job - I need to be making progress. Yet, Rockstar's invisible hand is so competently realised, so artisanally implemented, that I bow to its insistence that I live life properly and engage with all the systems suggested to me like a good little drone.
So, after being low-key brainwashed by the initial tutorialisation, it stands to reason that I'm open to Rockstar's other suggestions. And - right on cue - you get a mission early on that introduces you to what is perhaps the most hotly debated aspect of the game so far: the Criminal Profile. If you're unaware, this new mechanic is a bit like the Honour System in Red Dead Redemption 2. It's broken down into five levels: professional, hardened, violent, psycho, and irredeemable. If you hit that final bracket, irredeemable, you can never go back: it's essentially GTA 6's criminal version of 'being cancelled', only here there are real, serious consequences that will actually ruin your life forever.
The game tracks how you behave when you're playing as both Jason and Lucia. They have separate criminal profiles. If, for example, you fudge a robbery on a cartel's pill-shipping operation and fight for your life, you can certainly kill everyone in the room - that's still fine. This is still Grand Theft Auto, Rockstar isn't trying to make you play this game like Thief or Deus Ex or something. You can go for total stealth runs, but incapacitating enemies without killing them and getting away cleanly will only grant 'professional' points. You get the same assessment if you 'go loud' and aim for the hands, knees, feet of the people trying to kill you. I am currently about 30 hours in, and every single encounter has been either 'no casualties' or 'low casualties', and I promise I've not even been trying that hard to 'be good' (and there are always settings you can change to help you out if you're struggling, too).
There has been a certain amount of online discourse pointing towards this system as 'immersion ruining' or 'systematically inhibiting'. There's this idea that, in order to get a number of the game's 'good' endings, you need to play like a saint the whole way through the game. This is untrue. It's actually weighted more towards the opposite: in order to get the more nefarious ranks, you need to intentionally play like a sociopath. Wing a goon, see him lying on the floor in agony, and then go over and shoot his other kneecap? Yeah, you're going to get those unpopular purple devil points. Kick a dog in the street for no reason? Devil points. Taking a shotgun to a mall and opening fire on unarmed, un-implicated civilians? Devil points.
I'm enjoying the role-playing aspect of the game, because in my head-canon Jason and Lucia are doing what they can to survive. It may not be pretty, and I probably wouldn't want to know them in real life, but - as far as this work of fiction goes - I think playing them as criminals-on-the-run, trying to draw as little attention to themselves as possible is a great iteration of the series' core themes. I don't want to play as another Tommy Vercetti, or CJ, or Trevor. I want something different, and this game is giving it to me.
"The majority of our main characters are undeniably reprehensible on paper," explains Michael Wiafe, writer at Rockstar, in materials shared with Eurogamer ahead of the game's release. "[They're] full-blown criminals, but also decent human beings. Their moral makeup isn’t necessarily cut-and-dry, and we don’t attempt to make excuses for them. What’s important is how they resonate, no matter where you’re experiencing the game in the world." I think this shows, quite well, what the Criminal Profile mechanic sets out to achieve in GTA 6: it's Rockstar saying 'these people are forced into certain situations by us, the developers, but you get to figure out how they respond to what life is giving them'.
And you know what? I'm glad GTA 6 punishes you for playing like a psychopath. The world of Leonida is analogous to the real world, and things would start going wrong for you if you started attacking pedestrians randomly on the street. Other civilians and cops would start defending themselves and resisting you if you instigated a rampage of indiscriminate violence. The only time I've been victim to the devil icon in my game so far is when a Kingfisher accidentally shot out my (very expensive) windshield whilst aiming for Jason. So I kneecapped him, stole his beer, drank the whole bottle, then threw the bottle at his head. I acted like an idiot, and got treated as such. Good!
But I don't want to see that. I want to roleplay as Jason and Lucia and act as I think they would. I don't need the game telling me, like a little voice in my head, 'hm, actually, that was a pretty weird thing to do, we're going to write that down'. So I have turned the notifications off. It's a simple process: simply open Settings, and then navigate to UI, and head down to the 34/70 area and you'll see all the HUD notifications settings. I play with both Criminal Profile and Relationship settings turned off - I prefer to have all that happening in the background, ticking over as I play, rather than constantly reminding me there's some secret meter somewhere judging me for what I'm doing.
If my relationship is turning sour, I trust my instincts (and Rockstar's grounded, well-structured writing) to tell me that. Jason is getting a bit cold, Lucia doesn't want to jump my bones, like, all the time, the two aren't holding hands at every opportunity like lovesick puppies… Much like in my real-life relationships, I trust the process. And I think more people should, because the role-playing in this game is fantastic, and we've been given a real rich text to engage with. I think that the fact that certain corners of the internet are upset because they're being treated badly for being bad people is a better level of satire than anything GTA 6 has put in-game, to be honest.

item.title: Blizzard has officially unveiled Diablo 4's next live-service season: Season of Tyrael's Gambit. This is the ARPG's 16th season, and it follows on from the popular and well-received Season of Hell's Legacy. Read more
item.description:
Blizzard has officially unveiled Diablo 4's next live-service season: Season of Tyrael's Gambit. This is the ARPG's 16th season, and it follows on from the popular and well-received Season of Hell's Legacy.
In an unexpected move, Blizzard announced it's keeping some of the nostalgia-laiden content from the previous season, Season of Hell's Legacy, as a permanent addition. This is unusual, as the ephemeral nature of live seasons means new content goes away at the end of each season.
Season of Hell's Legacy paid tribute to Diablo's legacy and its 30th anniversary by introducing a lot of content inspired by previous Diablo games, chiefly Diablo 2. The list includes the return of iconic character Deckard Cain, a recreation of Old Tristram, and a big fight against the three Prime Evils - Diablo, Baal, and Mephisto - in their classic forms.
"We heard overwhelming requests for features from Season of Hell's Legacy to carry forward as permanent game features," Blizzard wrote in Season 16's announcement post. "While the entire season couldn't come along for the ride, we are implementing the following features with the launch of Season of Tyrael's Gambit that will carry forward in both Eternal and Seasonal realms."

Season of Tyrael's Gambit kicks off 1st December, so you still have time to access all of that in Diablo 4 until Season 15 ends. Certain things, such as craftable items, won't return, so you may as well try them while you can. That said, Blizzard is aware of the love some of those items have, and the developer said it may bring them back in the future.

item.title: You can do a lot of things in GTA 6: fishing, golfing, running, jumping, dancing, racing, roaming, shopping. It goes on! There's romancing, birdwatching, DIY, and even more besides. It really is an everything game. But GTA 6 isn't for everyone. Read more
item.description:
You can do a lot of things in GTA 6: fishing, golfing, running, jumping, dancing, racing, roaming, shopping. It goes on! There's romancing, birdwatching, DIY, and even more besides. It really is an everything game. But GTA 6 isn't for everyone.
So what if you were in the mood for some of this stuff but away from Leonida? Where else might you go? Consider this the slightly tenuous set-up, as we continue a week of Not-GTA, for us to highlight some of our favourite smaller games; brilliant lesser-known titles from the last 12 months or so that, in their own special way, beat GTA 6 at its own game.
Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch, Switch 2.
It's very sweet that the central, driving force of GTA 6 is the strained romance between Jason and Lucia. You are, essentially, playing a virtual matchmaker, helping these star-crossed lovers reconnect and rediscover each other after fate conspires to drive a wedge between them. But you know what's better than that? Being an actual matchmaker, matching icons on a grid and enjoying the microdose dopamine rush when you clear a line on a board.
So here's Titanium Court, which goes even further: with every line cleared, you come closer to escaping a weird, 80s-core fairy castle in a game that's partly telling a story about introspective self-doubt, and partly about warring fairies. If you're getting tired of texting your virtual lover every 10 minutes, perhaps try lighting a virtual cigarette in Titanium Court, instead - I've heard it does wonders for your health.
Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2.
How do you find out if you can really depend upon someone? That's a question at the heart of GTA 6. And the answer is: play Big Walk. There's nothing like gesturing through the window of a sound-proofed room hoping your friend or loved one will understand what two arms waggling around means. It means 'the high-pitched warbling sound plaque', obviously. Big Walk's wonderfully stripped-back world is also an antidote to GTA 6's maximal world. The silence and space in the game is absolutely the point. What will you fill it with?
It's not all roof repairs and late night paintjobs. Sometimes home improvement requires more drastic measures. And in Virtue and a Sledgehammer, that's taken to violent extremes. This is a game, in developers Selkie Harbour and Deconstructeam's words, about family, tradition, and being a misfit. Where an entire town - the protagonist's childhood home - faces a total spiritual teardown. Here, a brutal sledgehammer-swinging reckoning awaits as you unearth memories - some happy, some decidedly not - through violent destruction, cutting through mechanical human facsimiles with the faces of the ones you love. It's haunting, devastating stuff; a very different kind of do-it-yourself.
Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam).
You work, you sleep, and then you die. That's how it's got to be. So if you're going to toil mercilessly for the man, you can at least hope for an interesting employee. And what's more interesting than the weirdo threesome at the centre of Servant of the Lake?
Developer Rusty Lake's eponymous series returned this year with another macabre blend of point-and-click puzzling and room-escape-style adventure. And it's a corker. Perhaps not as dazzlingly experimental as some other recent entries, but it's still a delightfully grim time as you work through your three days of servitude, butlering for the oddball Vanderboom family. Beware the blood moon.
Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.
You work, you sleep, and then you die. But! What if you dream of breaking free? Escaping the chains of drudgery? That's the starting point of Denshattack!, a Jet Set Radio-inspired adventure all about sticking it to the man. Or, more specifically, a shady megacorp trying to suppress human ingenuity, creativity, and spirit. It is, as Dom put it in their five-star Denshattack! review, a game of "anti-capitalist, pop-punk optimism", which sees you careening across a colourful Japan - as a speeding, trick-flipping train, of all things - to bring the Miraidō corporation to its knees. Stylish and satisfying.
Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.
Umph-umph-umph-umph umph-umph-umph-umph. Oh yeah, that's the good stuff. If you want to shoot things and see them explode, and do that with immense satisfaction and a hypnotic, pulsating electronic soundtrack, this is the one. Sektori takes the feedback of a satisfying trigger pull and boils that down to its purest essence, often in spiralling, kaleidoscopic form. Hitting a full set of letters - M-I-R-A-G-E, S-E-K-T-O-R-I, etc. - summons a rainbow of action that feels like genuine ecstasy. Pure blasting and survival.
Available on: Android, iOS, PC (Steam), Switch, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.
Umph-umph-umph-umph umph-umph-umph-umph. But this time imagine it's a disco beat. Let's breathe in the night, bask in those pulsing lights, and pretend we'll live this moment forever. Or, you know, we'll just shuffle our way through the throng of the dancefloor like a massive game of sokoban. That latter's the premise of developer Miracle Tea's Club Soko; a game about traversing an underground nightclub - one shunt at a time - to discover the secrets it holds. And it's good 'un, bringing a thinkier rhythm to its pounding beat.
Most people think of fishing as a calm escape from the hustle and bustle of daily life - that's certainly the case of GTA 6. But relaxation, I say, is for posers, which brings us to How to Fish. In developer Dazed Games' silly, chaotic physics-based fishing sim, you're given an arsenal of guns to unload upon fish and foe alike. Beware the seagulls, who have learned to love the taste of human flesh over the bounty of humble chip shops. It's great fun, especially co-operatively, so grab some pals and have a blast.
Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.
Neasied, the island where Queen's Domain unfolds, might not be as dizzyingly expansive as some open-worlds, but the stuff it manages to pack into a relatively compact space is astonishing. This is a game crammed with secrets, rich with mystery; a world so dense with enigmas it's a joy to explore. There's more than a touch of FromSoftware to its broader retro-inspired combat rhythms, but there are hints of Zelda and Metroidvania too. It's one of the best games this year - full of surprise and wonder as its absurdly elaborate puzzle threads unfurl - and an extraordinary adventure.
Money too tight to mention? How about ditching the life of crime for a spot of restaurant entrepreneurialism? That's the idea behind Nivalis Night - and, actually, the life of crime is still an option. First seen in 2020 courier adventure Cloudpunk, Nivalis is a striking, sprawling cyberpunk dystopia of flying cars, neon lights, and suffocating smog that sets itself apart with its lo-fi style. And in this year's follow-up, you can finally get out of your car and live in the world. But it's not just a nifty first-person tycoon sim, it's a game of stories, and developer Ion Lands imbues its city with real warmth and humanity; a perfect accompaniment, it turns out, to all the Vangelis-like synths and sushi.
Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S.
There's street racing and then there's developer Milestone's Screamer. It's a narrative-focused racing game which leans into a far arcadier sort of drive compared to the more realistic Grand Theft Auto. It's also got a great anime aesthetic, so you can live out any MF Ghost fantasies you have tucked away. Or maybe Initial D for the drifting aficionados among you.
Okay, fine, so it's more of a slap than a punch, but developer Double Fine's Thank You Bus Driver still packs in more violence than you'd expect from a driving sim. This game jam experiment turned full release feels a bit like a first-person Crazy Taxi as you try and get passengers to their destination before time runs out. Happy passengers means more 'thank yous', which means more time for more pick-ups, and it's a brilliantly chaotic loop.
It's got bags of personality - its scrappy black-and-white doodle town and oddball passengers are a treat - and a bunch of neat hooks. Most notably, HQ intermittently imposes new rules - no talking! No toenail clipping! - which is where slaps come in. Rulebreakers need discipline if you don't want to lose your 'thank yous', so you spin around and wallop them about the chops. Just try not to drive off the road.
Available on: PC (Steam), PlayStation 5.
Sure, Leonida's landscape holds its own kind of sunkissed beauty, but The Game Bakers has created something really special with Cairn. It might be a game focused on mountain climbing, but it's hard not to stop and admire the view whenever you reach the next plateau. As you make your way up Mount Kami, you're greeted with almost constant lovely views, some of the most gorgeous vistas released this year. Cairn is the sort of game that warrants putting the controller down and just taking the sights in for a moment or two.
As a doctor of dubious repute once said, where we're going, we don't need roads! So wave goodbye to metropolitan squalor, farewell to suburban suffocation, and hello the great outdoors. Over the Hill, the follow-up to Funselektor's brilliant Art of Rally, is all about off-road roaming through the vast, untamed wilderness. It's a game of purposeful meandering and patient delights and you explore the secrets of, among other places, its starlit deserts and rolling forest hills. You'll bounce your 4x4 over rocks, crawl sluggishly up hills, and winch through squelching mud, and it's all so slow. That's deliberate though. And as the result, amid the gentle strum of soothing guitar, is a wonderfully meditative game.
Available on: PC (Steam, Epic, GOG).
There are few other games released this year that nail the ruthlessness of vehicle-to-vehicle combat like Airframe Ultra. An absolutely gorgeous battle-racer in which you take control of a bulky airframe. You can smack the daylights out of other riders with chains, bats, and other makeshift melee weapons. Failing that, ramming into people at full speed works wonders too. A gritty game that pleases the eye and nourishes the violent soul.
Life, eh? One minute it's all Leonida sunshine and motorboating, the next you're on the run. But it's how you deal with each roll of the dice that matters. And that's very much the premise of Cosmo D's wonderfully weird Moves of the Diamond Hand. It's back to the jazz-drenched, oddball world of Off-Peak City we go, this time as election day looms. The legendary Circus X has returned to town and you want a place in its show. What follows is a first-person narrative adventure that takes the tabletop RPG-inspired dice-throwing of Cosmo D's acclaimed 2022 game Betrayal at Club Low and turns it into something richer, deeper, wilder, and weirder. And yes, it's got a killer soundtrack.
Available on: PC (Steam, Epic), PlayStation 5, Switch 2, Xbox Series X/S.
I see you smirking, pal - cut it out. Early on in GTA 6 you're tasked with hosing off a boat in the marina. And if that scratches an unknown itch within you, PowerWash Simulator 2 has all the nozzle blasting you could hope for. Yes, it's a slightly older one, but all 2026's DLC means it still feels new. Even more grimy buildings and filthy objects are waiting for a hero with a soap dispenser, just begging for a deep clean. Is that you? Then live your dream!
Browsing the tourist traps and fashion emporiums for the next big look is all well and good, but have you ever considered taking matters into your own hands? Dressmaking might not seem like the most appealing way to spend your time if you're not particularly into wearing dresses or seamstressing. (It's me, I'm that person.) However, Dressmaker and the sheer amount of clothing combinations it makes possible are a very pleasant surprise.
Weaved throughout it all is a story that sees you designing dresses for different characters and the events they're attending, then stitching your ideas to life piece by piece with tactile minigames, And you can design your own dresses too! I can only imagine GTA 6's Jason might even enjoy designing a dress or two for Lucia if he had Dressmaker on his JoyStation...
Creator, writer, director, composer, and 'perceptual architect' Johannes Zuch's Tenebrae Lux might be wowing the critics in GTA 6, but for my money this year's best game-within-a-game is Forbidden Solitaire. It's 2019 and you've stumbled upon an old copy of notorious CD-ROM adventure Forbidden Solitaire. It was pulled from the shelves amid some mysterious deaths, but that won't stop you from playing. What follows is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn - told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, even a recreation of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show - which brilliantly evokes the 90s multimedia boom with its lurid, awkward pre-rendered game-in-a-game visuals. It also, in case you're wondering, plays a damn good game of solitaire.
I like birds. I like them so much that it's at the top of my bucket list to find a Wonga Pigeon one day. So, you can imagine how I felt finding out that GTA 6 has over 60 birds to spot, alongside binoculars and a phone camera to fulfil my bird-watching dreams.
Before GTA 6 however, there came a lovely little multiplayer game called Flock Around developed by Friend Shaped Games that lets you explore multiple biomes while trying to snap photographs of birds from around the world and fill out your guide book. I was enamoured by its simple loop of wandering around and waiting for birds to strike a perfect pose, take selfies with them, and maybe even watching them empty their insides all over your friends. I don't think it's possible to be pooped on by a bird in GTA 6, so by default, Flock Around takes the crown as one of the best games for snapping pics of birds this year.
Available on: PC (Steam, itch.io).
It's not hard to have a better cleaning regimen than GTA 6's Jason: the man apparently isn't aware his nethers need a wash too. But designer Robert Yang's Rinse and Repeat's has a solution for those struggling at showertime: get someone else to help you. Rinse and Repeat is a "steamy first-person showering game ... about consent and safety" and got a remaster earlier this year as part of Yang's Radiator Forever compilation. Yang's award-winning work frequently explores queer subculture, and the NSFW compilation also contains three other games - Hurt Me Plenty, Succulent, and Stick Shift - with more to follow. Better yet, it's completely free.
Available on: iOS, PC (Steam).
Forget cracking safes in GTA 6, what about cracking the codes in a machine that seems to be, well, more than it seems? This is the hook in Inkle's TR-49, a game about a machine that once lurked in the depths of Bletchley Park's legendary codebreaking vaults, alongside the Enigma Machine. This machine works differently. It's effectively an archive you search around using codes in the format of letter-letter, number-number, hence TR-49. But the codes you use and what you find, and how you find them: that's up to you. And sure, there's probably not gold bullion on the other side of this code, but perhaps there's something even more rewarding.

item.description:
One GTA 6 player has put in the legwork and found that a shocking number of buildings across Leonida are freely accessible.
Per a Reddit post by Aileos, 1,563 of the game's 5,588 buildings can be entered, coming in at 27.97 percent of structures in the game. Some of those are ones you'd expect of course: stores, banks, and the like. But plenty of them may surprise you. The next time you're walking across a neighbourhood, pick a house and just walk inside… in-game, of course.
Plenty of the best secrets in GTA 6 can be found off the beaten trail. Random drops of illicit goods can be found all over the place. So, if you're having a blast making your way through the game, take an hour or so just to wander around the place and take in the scenery.
If you are in the market for some help through the game, Eurogamer's GTA 6 walkthrough is a great source of helpful information. Likewise, our page on all the GTA 6 cheats is a great help for those in need.

item.title: As part of The Witcher and Cyberpunk studio CD Projekt Red's recent Q3 earnings report, the developer offered some updates on upcoming game The Witcher 4. Read more
item.description:
As part of The Witcher and Cyberpunk studio CD Projekt Red's recent Q3 earnings report, the developer offered some updates on upcoming game The Witcher 4.
During an earnings call yesterday, the studio revealed it had signed a new partnership deal with Sony regarding marketing rights to The Witcher 4, as well as to extend "the presence" of CD Projekt Red's other games across the PlayStation Store and PlayStation Plus.
"Just today, we signed new partnership agreements with Sony Interactive Entertainment covering the presence of our games on PlayStation and in PlayStation Plus subscriptions, as well as our collaboration during the upcoming Witcher 4 marketing campaign," said studio CFO Piotr Nielubowicz. "This cooperation will support our business and financial outlook in this and future years."
Nielubowicz didn't elaborate on what exactly that means for The Witcher 4's marketing, but perhaps it could enable Sony to advertise the action-RPG as a PlayStation game, similar to the Grand Theft Auto 6 'plays best on PlayStation' campaign. But seeing as The Witcher 4 is currently targeting a 2028 release, we may not find out what form that agreement takes for some time.
That said, looking at similar marketing agreements from Sony's recent history, we can probably expect The Witcher 4 to show up during Sony State of Play presentations or even have dedicated PlayStation-focused showcases. The Witcher 4 footage may also be specified as being captured on PlayStation hardware - something we already saw with The Witcher 4 tech demo last year. Perhaps we'll see Witcher-themed accessories and PlayStation hardware, too.
This is a notable shift for CDPR, which has historically had close ties to Xbox. Cyberpunk 2077's big Keanu Reeves reveal (as Johnny Silverhand) took place on Xbox's E3 2019 stage, and The Witcher 3's reveal happened on Microsoft's E3 2013 stage. Going further back, Xbox 360 was the only console The Witcher 2 was released on.
During the same earnings call, CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski said that we should expect the leap between The Witcher 3 and The Witcher 4 to be similar to that between GTA 5 and GTA 6, while also praising Rockstar's approach to marketing its record-breaking new game.
